newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader votes, says West "really loves me".
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader votes, says West "really loves me".

text.p: Hardline Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, compared by critics to Europe's worst dictators, on Sunday voted in a referendum to tighten his grip and hailed Charles de Gaulle, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Margaret Thatcher as his heroes.

"I really respect the West and it really loves me -- as much as it is able to," he told Reuters after casting his ballot to extend his term beyond 2000 and widen his authority on rival institutions in the former Soviet republic.

"Apart from political rhetoric, there are no difficulties with the West," he added after chatting for 30 minutes with reporters who have descended on the country of 10 million situated between Russia and Poland.
Referring to his long-running conflict with parliament and the constitutional court, he told reporters: "After the referendum all these fights will vanish."
He attacked parliament for scuppering a compromise deal brokered by Russia on Friday and said he would act according to the result of the voting.
The main question out of seven put to the voters is approval of a new constitution extending his term in office and widening his powers.
"I do not doubt that foreign states and Russia will recognise the referendum as legitimate," he said.
Lukashenko's policies have drawn widespread criticism from Western human rights organisations and international lending bodies have withdrawn funding pending faster reforms.

But on Sunday he was in determined mood. He sped up to a sports academy in suburban Minsk in his presidential limousine -- plate number 0001 MI -- to cast his ballot in a referendum which has thrown Belarus into political turmoil.
The words of the 42-year-old leader, clearly in a good mood as voting raced ahead in the referendum which he is expected to win, were a far cry from his previous statements on the West.
He bitterly opposes NATO's plans to expand eastwards, and once called the Western alliance a "dreadful monster".
"I am not afraid of anything. Why should I be afraid of NATO expansion eastwards?" he said.
"Investment is reaching Belarus. I support those who want economic cooperation. Believe me, the political rhetoric will vanish," he said.
Asked who his heroes were, he said: "De Gaulle, Roosevelt and I also respect the female leader Margaret Thatcher".
Parliamentary speaker Semyon Sharetsky, spokesman for the opposition, has compared Lukashenko to Germany's Adolf Hitler, Italy's Benito Mussolini and Spain's Francisco Franco.

Lukashenko himself has been quoted in at least one interview as praising Hitler. Late on Saturday, Russia's ORT television broadcast what sounded like a recording of his voice over pictures of Auschwitz concentration camp saying Hitler brought order and stability to pre-war Germany.

But he told reporters on Sunday: "It was a falsification, an edited track. It wasn't made by journalists. You know my policies, you know my approach, and my judgements about fascism in general. I never said this. Never."
The tall, angular, moustachioed Lukashenko was in conciliatory mood about his opponents in parliament, who have been trying to remove him from office by impeachment.
"The new constitution allows me to dissolve parliament after a month if we do not reach agreement," he said, but added: "I will not dissolve it because we will find harmony."

If his draft is approved at the polls, the constitution will be changed to create an upper house of parliament of 64 representatives and a lower house of 110 deputies. His term in office will also be extended by two years.
Lukashenko said on Sunday: "A country in which there is democratic development on the basis of order and discipline, needs this constitution."
